> A plasma speaker that turns audio signals into sound by modulating an electric arc. I want to explore how high-voltage electronics can become a musical instrument, with adjustable tones and simple melodies. The project will include a custom audio control circuit and high-voltage section.

### 2026-10-22 – ## Designing the Gromofon driver

**7.93h**

## Designing the Gromofon driver

This session focused on researching and designing the electronics for Gromofon, my plasma speaker project. I compared existing designs, worked on a schematic in KiCad, and put together a preliminary parts cart.

### Research and design choices

I studied Plasma Channel’s plasma speaker video and Conrad’s TL494-based plasma speaker article. I compared their approaches to driving a flyback transformer and looked into possible causes of MOSFET failures, including voltage spikes, overheating and transformer saturation.

I chose to use an ESP32 instead of a 555 timer to generate the control signal. The current design uses a TC4420 gate driver between the ESP32 and the power MOSFET.

### Schematic progress

I drafted a circuit containing:
- A 24 V power input with filtering capacitors.
- An L7812 regulator to supply 12 V to the gate driver.
- A TC4420 with local decoupling capacitors.
- An IRFP260N MOSFET and a gate resistor.
- A pull-down resistor on the PWM input.
- An RCD clamp intended to limit voltage spikes from the transformer.

![schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/31f88ad37a41fb97d61e48512709e33d9d7ad015f33b683d355af212aea900f3.png)

During the schematic review, I identified further changes, including adding a gate-to-source pull-down resistor and improving the regulator’s local decoupling. The clamp component values are still provisional because the transformer has not been selected.

I plan to assemble the prototype on perfboard, with short connections around the gate driver and MOSFET.

### Parts and budget

I checked my available parts and found an L7812CV regulator. I also have screw terminals and plan to reuse a suitable heatsink.

I assembled a preliminary parts cart and compared prices and alternatives. This helped me spot unnecessary quantities and a resistor value that did not match the schematic. I also looked for more suitable capacitors for decoupling and the RCD clamp.

![cart1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/4816363fad93dba0e234959c88e17028d2d4320ccd42a0cdf343ac66f0f70811.png)

![cart2](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/45152fc19a6b460927a614a827af6d665f74174ba92d337ed1a0be2692eec31e.png)

### Main unresolved issue

Choosing the transformer is currently the biggest challenge. I researched CRT flyback transformers, AC high-voltage transformers and the possibility of winding one myself. I found several inexpensive listings, but their descriptions do not yet provide enough information to confirm compatibility with my driver.

### Additional research outside the timelapses — approximately 3 hours

Outside the recorded sessions, I spent approximately three hours researching the project. I read articles, watched relevant YouTube videos, and checked component datasheets and supplier listings.

I focused on MOSFET selection, gate drivers, flyback transformers and protection against voltage spikes. I also compared component prices and availability to help keep the design within budget.

This research helped me refine the circuit concept and identify which specifications still need to be confirmed before ordering parts.

### Next steps

- Select a transformer and confirm its specifications.
- Finish the schematic corrections.
- Finalize the parts list within the project budget.
- Define conservative PWM limits for the selected transformer.
- Test the low-voltage control section before connecting the HV stage.

### 2026-10-24 – # Entry 2: firmware, BOM and README

**8h**

# Entry 2: firmware, BOM and README

This session I moved from drawing the circuit to working on the firmware, the parts list and the README.

The ESP32 handles signal generation and audio modulation, so I started with the firmware. It pairs over Bluetooth as "Gromofon", converts the incoming audio to mono, low-pass filters it and resamples it for an 8 kHz modulation update rate. The audio changes the PWM duty on GPIO18, which will connect to the TC4420 gate driver. The default carrier is 25 kHz with 10-bit PWM and a 5% duty cap. There is also a 440 Hz test tone and a constant-duty mode, so I can check the output without Bluetooth.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/bbdb9dc790ff360e165888140aa9799cedd5003029a755d705eff2c12d08d08b.png)

A large part of the firmware work was handling interruptions and errors. Output starts disabled and requires an "a" command over serial to arm it. After arming, it ramps up over one second. The firmware disarms when it detects missing audio, Bluetooth source changes, buffer faults or a missed control deadline. There is a task watchdog too.

I limited pulse duration in microseconds as well as duty cycle. Transformer saturation depends on the applied voltage and pulse duration, together with the transformer design, so a duty percentage alone is not enough to choose an operating point. The transformer has not been selected or measured yet, so I left the pulse limit at zero. This blocks output in the normal build until a limit has been established. There is a separate bench mode with a 3 µs limit, only for inspecting the GPIO signal with the power stage disconnected. That value is not a validated transformer setting.

Both the default and bench configurations compiled successfully with Arduino-ESP32 3.3.8 and ESP32-A2DP 1.8.11. Neither has been tested on the complete hardware yet.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/19b98327cc1b23ab8a9b8c09d1b7a25e1d474be08ea34033b3393c14a962907e.png)

Next I worked on the parts list. The current shopping list includes five IRFP260N MOSFETs with spares, a TC4420 driver, a fast diode for the RCD clamp, capacitors, resistors and DIP sockets. I priced the parts from a Polish shop and converted the VAT-inclusive prices at about 3.90 PLN per dollar. The listed parts total about $21.16, excluding shipping.

This is still a preliminary order rather than a finished BOM. Some quantities are whole packs, and the transformer, heatsink, perfboard, wire and remaining schematic changes are not included yet.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/91c09d96061a0f43952786814957b28b63ce8f851862c4ec8d4ed78305401ddb.png)

Finally, I prepared a firmware README with the build versions, serial commands, settings and fault behavior. I kept the comments in the code short and moved the longer explanations into the README. I also prepared the firmware folder structure and a .gitignore to keep build files out of the repository. The main README now describes the current circuit, the preliminary budget and what still needs testing.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/19d34f73254cff08b0401d1105a0ce65563ae03655796bbdc561b57499883248.png)

Next I need to select the transformer, finish the schematic corrections and make the BOM match it. After that I can plan the perfboard layout and test the GPIO output with the power stage disconnected before building the high-voltage section in week 8.

## Further revisions — 3 hours

I spent another three hours refining the schematic, BOM and README, and checking that the project files agreed with each other.

On the schematic, I worked on the gate-to-source pull-down, and the component labels. I also reviewed the placement of the existing decoupling capacitors around the regulator and gate driver. The RCD clamp values are still provisional because the transformer has not been selected.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/32b6471b2ea7cae7b7a7a60097bcb3e6e107aff9c63033a0818bdd5dc4ad94fd.png)

I checked the BOM against the schematic, identified the missing 22 kΩ resistor and compared gate-driver prices.  I kept five MOSFETs, including spares, and clarified that I already have perfboard, low-voltage wire and a heatsink.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/63ca03d2553b63c8eb8997fe8c48aa69753759186a24a596ea57b9c9e522a493.png)

I updated the main README to reflect the $30 funding request and explain that I will cover additional costs myself. I also expanded the explanation of the transformer search. I am looking through local listings first, with an inexpensive AliExpress transformer or winding my own as possible alternatives that still need investigation. I reviewed the repository for outdated descriptions and differences between the documentation and parts list.
